[[File:Stancari, Vittorio Francesco – Schedae mathematicae post ejus obitum collectae ejusdem Observationes astronomicae, 1713 – BEIC 4713493.jpg|thumb|''Schedae mathematicae post ejus obitum collectae ejusdem Observationes astronomicae'', 1713]]
'''Vittorio Francesco Stancari''' (29 July 1678{{snd}}28 March 1709) was a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Bologna]] who undertook research into the measurement of sounds, and into optics and hydrostatics.

==Career==
Vittorio Francesco Stancari was born in Bologna in 1678.  In 1698 he became a professor of mathematics at the University of Bologna.<ref name=Treccani/>
Stancari was one of a group of young men at the University who became interested in the techniques of [[Cartesian geometry]] and [[differential calculus]], and who engaged in experiments and astronomical observation. Others were [[Eustachio Manfredi]], his brother [[Gabriele Manfredi]] and [[Giuseppe Sentenziola Verzaglia]].
Of these, Gabriele Manfredi developed the most advanced understanding of mathematics.{{sfn|Feingold|Brotons|2006|p=133}}
Stancari was awarded the chair of infinitesimal calculus in Bologna in 1708.{{sfn|Olschki|1996|p=307}}
He died in Bologna in 1709, aged about 31.<ref name=Treccani/>

==Work==

Stancari's dissertations and manuscripts show that he applied [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibnizian]] [[calculus]] to problems of physics, 
hydrodynamics, meteorology and mechanics.{{sfn|Olschki|1996|p=307}}
He was also aware of Sir [[Isaac Newton]]'s ''Principia Mathematica'', 
and discussed Newton in lectures before the ''[[Accademia degli Inquieti]]'' in Bologna.{{sfn|Feingold|2004|p=81}}

Stancari developed a method of measuring the pitch of sound in 1706, using foil that was excited into vibration by rotating toothed wheels.<ref name=Treccani>{{cite encyclopedia
|title        = Stancari, Vittorio Francesco
|url          = https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/vittorio-francesco-stancari
|encyclopedia = Enciclopedia on line
|location     = Rome
|publisher    = [[Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana]]
|access-date  = 29 July 2025
|language     = it
}}</ref> Working in the observatory founded by [[Luigi Ferdinando Marsili|Count Marsigli]],<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hg5BAQAAMAAJ|title=Dizionario biografico universale|volume=5|first=Felice|last=Scifoni|publisher=David Passigli|location=Florence|year=1849|page=172}}</ref> Stancari and Eustachio Manfredi discovered the comet [[C/1707 W1]] in the evening of 25 November 1707. They described it as visible to the naked eye, white, irregular and with a short, faint tail. It had the same apparent size as Jupiter.{{sfn|Kronk|1999|p=389}}

Stancari experimented with [[Guillaume Amontons]]' air thermometer, where air in the bulb pushes up a column of mercury as it expands due to rising temperature.  He discovered that the humidity of the air in the bulb had a significant effect on the readings.{{sfn|Camuffo|Jones|2002|p=299}}
